title: Chemoenzymatic synthesis of pentalenolactones via stereoselective Riley oxidation by engineered P450_BM3

paper_content.abstract: Riley oxidation is a powerful method for introducing oxygen functionality but typically relies on toxic reagents and generally lacks enantiocontrol. This limitation has historically restricted the utility of this transformation for the direct asymmetric construction of complex scaffolds. Here, we show that fusion library screening and directed evolution enable the highly enantio- and diastereoselective Riley-type oxidation of a cis-diquinane substrate catalyzed by engineered P450 BM3. This enzymatic desymmetrization strategy provides streamlined access to key chiral cis-diquinane building block on a gram scale, facilitating rapid downstream diversification. Furthermore, by merging this enzymatic desymmetrization with chemical ring formation and late-stage biosynthetic oxidation, we achieve asymmetric total synthesis of pentalenolactone D and neo-pentalenolactone D. This work highlights the power of integrating protein engineering with synthetic chemistry to synthesis of complex natural products.
paper_content.introduction:
Natural products and drugs featuring a cis-diquinane scaffold typically possess architecturally complex frameworks and display notable biological activities1–5. Natural products containing the diquinane motif have long attracted the interest of synthetic chemists as targets for total synthesis6,7. However, efficient, and scalable preparation of chiral diquinane fragments remains a significant challenge. The C2-symmetric cis-diquinane core represents a meso framework that can, in principle, be efficiently accessed via desymmetrization strategies (Fig. 1A). Among previously reported strategies, desymmetrization by allylic oxidation has emerged as a powerful method for the synthesis of enantioenriched allylic alcohols (Fig. 1B)8–12. However, reported reactions of this type have thus far been limited to relatively simple substrates, and no examples of enantioselective Riley-type hydroxylation have been described to date13–21. Given the previous success of enzyme library screening and directed evolution strategies in synthetic applications22–34, we hypothesized that enzyme-catalyzed oxidation could offer a more effective solution for structurally complex substrates.

In this work, we develop a synthetic approach starting from an accessible, unsubstituted meso cis-diquinane, in which oxidative desymmetrization is employed to construct a chiral cis-diquinane core (Fig. 1C). This approach enables enantioselective Riley-type direct hydroxylation catalyzed by engineered P450 BM3. A readily accessible meso substrate bearing carbonyl and olefin functionalities serves as a versatile intermediate for downstream functionalization. Through subsequent side-chain installation, cyclization, and late-stage oxidation catalyzed by biosynthetic enzymes, this strategy provides access to the tricyclic skeleton and enables the asymmetric total synthesis of pentalenolactone D and neo-pentalenolactone D.
paper_content.results:
We selected the known compound 135 as a substrate to investigate the enzymatic desymmetrizing allylic oxidation (Fig. 2). By screening oxidative transformations using our oxidase libraries of P450 monooxygenases and α-ketoglutarate-dependent dioxygenases33, we identified that the wild-type P450 BM3 and its F87V mutant afforded the major hydroxylated product 2 with 73% e.e. and 1.6:1 d.r., 88% e.e. and 4.3: 1 d.r., respectively. Guided by the crystal structure of P450 BM3 (PDB: 1JPZ)36, we rationally selected and mutated several residues predicted to play critical roles in shaping the active-site pocket size and modulating substrate–residue interactions. Building upon the F87V mutant, we performed two rounds of saturation mutagenesis at residues 47 and 49. The resulting variant, AAO3, exhibited improved enantioselectivity and diastereoselectivity, affording compound 2 with 98% e.e. and 6.9:1 d.r. Mutations at positions 78 and 82 individually did not lead to further enhancement in selectivity. Inspired by Reetz’s strategy of combinatorial active-site mutagenesis37, we introduced a double mutation at these two positions. The resulting mutant, AAO4, significantly improved the diastereoselectivity (>20:1 d.r.) of the reaction while maintaining high enantioselectivity. We further achieved gram-scale synthesis of compound 2 with excellent diastereoselectivity and enantioselectivity. In addition, the absolute configuration of compound 2 was unambiguously confirmed by X-ray crystal structure of its derivative 4.

To showcase the applicability of the chiral cis-diquinane scaffold, we employed it in the total synthesis of pentalenolactone D and neo-pentalenolactone D3. Biological studies of the pentalenolactones have shown that they selectively inhibit glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate dehydrogenase, suggesting their potential as lead compounds for the development of novel antibiotic agents38–42. Accordingly, these pharmacologically important natural products have garnered significant attention from synthetic chemists43–60. Here, the retrosynthetic analysis of pentalenolactone D and neo-pentalenolactone D was undertaken (Fig. 3). Our retrosynthetic logic features a three-stage synthesis to access the target natural products. Initially, late-stage oxidation of biosynthetically recognizable 1-deoxypentalenic acid (7) enable the synthesis of pentalenolactones. In the next stage, 1-deoxypentalenic acid (7) can be obtained from pentalenene (8) via Riley oxidation. In addition, the skeleton of pentalenene (8) can be constructed by 9 through a sequence of Cu-catalyzed 1,4-addition and intramolecular alkylation. Compound 9 can be obtained from compound 2, generated via enzymatic desymmetrizing allylic oxidation, through an enantioretentive elimination. The key feature of this retrosynthetic analysis lies in the integration of engineered P450 BM3-catalyzed oxidation, chemical cyclization, and late-stage biosynthetic enzymatic oxidation.

Our synthetic route is depicted in Fig. 4, which commenced with commercially available compound 10. Although the synthesis of compound 1 had been previously reported via a three-step sequence35, we employed the method reported by H. Lebel and co-workers61 to access compound 1 directly from 10 in a single step, thereby improving step economy. With a substantial quantity of 1 in hand, compound 2 was prepared on a gram scale via our developed enzymatic desymmetrizing allylic oxidation, exhibiting high enantio- and diastereoselectivity. Simmons-Smith reaction of 2 afforded compound 11 which was subsequently subjected to hydrogenation to furnish the diol 12. Attempts to achieve selective oxidation of diol 12 to the compound 13 were undertaken. However, extensive screening of various oxidation conditions (DMP, PCC, SO3·Pyridine, etc.) lacked selectivity. Fortunately, treatment 12 with Ph3C+BF4- successfully afforded the desired compound 13 with excellent selectivity. The inability of the sterically congested carbocation to approach the hydroxyl group adjacent to the geminal dimethyl substituents may account for this observation. Then, we sought to dehydration of the C1-hydroxyl group of 13 to generate an alkene, followed by isomerization to afford enone 9. Presumably due to the presence of the geminal dimethyl group, dehydration reagents such as Burgess reagent and Martin sulfurane failed to yield the desired compound 9. Consequently, compound 13 was converted to the xanthate ester 14 and subsequent pyrolysis afforded 15. Notably, compound 15 underwent smoothly alkene isomerization under the condition to furnish enone 9. It is noteworthy that the elimination proceeded with retention of chirality. Conjugate addition to enone 9 proceeded smoothly, establishing the crucial quaternary carbon center. Subsequent desilylation afforded compound 16. Hydrogenation of 16 using Crabtree’s catalyst proceeded with moderate stereoselectivity, and the intermediate alcohol was tosylated to yield compound 17. Exposure of compound 17 under basic condition induced cyclization, affording the tricyclic product 18. Compound 18 was elaborated over two steps to furnish the natural product pentalenene (8). Pentalenene (8) was transformed to 1-deoxypentalenic acid (7) accessible to recognition by biosynthetic enzymes via allylic oxidation with SeO2, followed by Pinnick oxidation.

With 1-deoxypentalenic acid (7) in hand, we proceeded to investigate late-stage biosynthetic enzyme-catalyzed oxidation based on native enzymes originally reported by the group of D. E. Cane (Fig. 5)62,63. Among them, the α-ketoglutarate-dependent dioxygenase PtlH catalyzed hydroxylation at C11 of 1-deoxypentalenic acid (7), providing this transformation in high yield with exclusive regio- and stereoselectivity. Introduction the oxidation state is essential for achieving the total syntheses of pentalenolactone D (5) and neo-pentalenolactone D (6). Then, the resulting 19 was oxidized under Dess–Martin periodinane condition to provide ketone 20. Due to the observed instability of compound 20 on silica gel, it was carried forward without purification. Chemical Baeyer–Villiger oxidation conditions (m-CPBA, H2O2, etc.) proved unsatisfactory, which might be due to regioselectivity issues and incompatibility with the alkene moiety. Consequently, enzymatic Baeyer–Villiger oxidation was pursued. Screening of our Baeyer–Villiger monooxygenases library confirmed that the coexpression of PntE or PtlE, and the phosphite dehydrogenase Opt13 for NADPH (reduced form of nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide phosphate) regeneration in a single E. coli BL21(DE3) strain allowed remarkable regioselectivity to afford pentalenolactone D (5) and neo-pentalenolactone D (6), respectively. Other Baeyer–Villiger monooxygenases (AndJ, Rhodo, EthA, AusZ, etc), however, displayed no catalytic activity toward this substrate. Thus, through late-stage oxidation mediated by biosynthetic enzymes, we accomplished the asymmetric total syntheses of pentalenolactone D (5) and neo-pentalenolactone D (6).
paper_content.methods:
Generation of pET22b(+)-P450 BM3 and pRSF-Opt13 Co-expression Vector
The respective gene fragment of P450 BM3 was synthesized and assembled directly into pET22b(+) between NdeI and XhoI by Universe Gene Technology (Tianjin) Co. Ltd to yield vector pET22b(+)-P450 BM3. Opt-13 gene were inserted between NcoI and XhoI restriction sites of pRSF-1b to yield vector pRSF-Opt13. The resulting vectors pET22b(+)-P450 BM3 and pRSF-Opt13 were used to co-transform competent E. coli strain BL21(DE3).

Gram-Scale Synthesis of Compound 2
An overnight culture of E. coli BL21(DE3) cells harboring pET-22b(+)-based vector for expressing P450 BM3 (AAO4) and pRSF-Opt13 plasmid was used to inoculate 500 mL TB media (in 2L Erlenmeyer flask) containing 50 µg/mL kanamycin, 50 µg/mL ampicillin. The cultures were shaken at 250 rpm at 37 ˚C until an optical density of OD600=0.7–1.0 was reached. The cultures were cooled to 20°C (20 min) and then induced with 5-aminolevulinic, IPTG and FeSO4·7H2O to final concentrations of 1.0 mM, 0.5 mM and 0.05 mM, respectively. The cultures were shaken at 250 rpm at 20°C for a further 20 h. Cells were harvested by centrifugation (4°C, 15 min, 2100 × g), resuspended in 50 mM KPi (pH=8.00) to an OD600=10 into a 2L Erlenmeyer flask. Cells were disrupted by sonication (20 min, cycle= 1s on/2s off, 50% amplitude) and pelleted by centrifugation (4°C, 15 min, 2100 × g). The supernatant was used directly for subsequent reactions. Reactions were carried out in parallel across twelve 2L Erlenmeyer flasks, each charged with the following amounts of substrate and reagents. A pre-dissolved solution of 1 (300 mg, 2.0 mmol, 4.0 mM final concentration) in 25 mL DMSO was added to the lysate, followed by Na2NADP (250 mg, 0.32 mmol, 0.16 equiv.) and Na2HPO4∙5H2O (6.25 g, 28.9 mmol, 14.5 equiv.). The flask was shaken at 150 rpm at 23°C under air for 20 h. Then, 25 g NaCl was added to flask and the mixture was extracted with EtOAc (400 mL × 3). The combined organic extracts of twelve 2L Erlenmeyer flasks from the twelve parallel reactions were washed with sat. aq. NaHCO3 (400 mL), dried over anhydrous Na2SO4, and concentrated in vacuo. The crude material was purified by flash column chromatography to yield compound 2 of 1.60 g (44%) as yellow oil.

reviewer_comments.reviewer_1:
The manuscript by Li and coworkers report an excellent strategy to constructed enantio- and diastereoselectivity chiral cis-diquinane via Riley-type oxidation by engineered P450BM3. This work achieved the total syntheses of the natural products pentalenolactone D and neo-pentalenolactone D by combining chemical synthesis with enzyme-catalyzed synthesis.
Here I have a few questions for the author:
1. The description of protein engineering is relatively brief and lacks the rationale for selecting mutation sites regarding the section on mutation engineering of enzymes. For instance, the experimental design in which saturation mutagenesis was performed on residues 47 and 49 using the F87V mutant as a template (lines 58-61 in manuscript) lacks a clear justification. It is unclear what evidence or reasoning guided the decision-making to (i) employ the F87V mutant specifically, and (ii) focus the saturation efforts on residues 47 and 49. Providing this information is crucial for evaluating the soundness of the experimental strategy. In the section "Library screening of P450BM3 mutants" within SI, the 35 P450BM3 mutants are mentioned. The description lacks the precise criteria used for their selection. Please clarify the screening methodology and ensure that the corresponding experimental results for these mutants are fully presented in SI.
2.The manuscript describes the first asymmetric total syntheses of pentalenolactone D and neo-pentalenolactone D, which indeed represents a highly innovative achievement. To better contextualize the significance of this work, we inquire whether there have been any prior synthetic efforts toward these or closely related compounds. Furthermore, given the multi-step nature of the synthetic route, we seek clarification on the overall yield. Finally, we are interested in the authors' perspective on the potential of this strategy to serve as a general method for preparing this class of natural products.
3.The manuscript mentions that pentanolactones can specifically inhibit glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate dehydrogenase and have potential antibacterial effects. The manuscript cites three references related to the study of such compounds, but all of which were conducted 30 years ago. May I ask if there are any recent research results to support the antibiotic activity of pentanolactones. Is there any relevant antibacterial activity test in this work to confirm the antibacterial activity of the compound？Finally, a forward-looking discussion on the therapeutic potential of this compound class as novel antibiotics, particularly within the current landscape of antimicrobial resistance, would greatly enhance the impact and relevance of the study.
4.The manuscript would benefit from a careful proofread to correct a number of minor linguistic errors. kPi-KPi, TCL-TLC. Several variations were noted in the expression of rotational speed values (e.g., "4200 rpm" vs. "4,200 rpm"). To maintain rigorous scientific presentation and adhere to journal style, please select one formatting of numbers (e.g., use of commas).
reviewer_comments.reviewer_2:
The authors report a chemoenzymatic synthesis of pentalenolactone D and its regioisomer neo-pentalenolactone D. First, the authors utilize a p450BM3 enzyme and through directed evolution achieve highly selective desymmetrization of diquinanes by enzymatic Riley oxidation. Second, chemical synthesis is used for a concise synthesis of triquinanes pentalenene and 1-deoxypentalenic acid. Finally, using known biosynthetic enzymes in the biosynthesis of pentalenolactone, the chemoenzymatic synthesis was achieved. These enzymes include an alpha-KG dependent hydroxylase, PtlH, and the regiodivergent Baeyer-Villiger monooxygenases (PntE and PtlE).
By combining synthetic chemistry with enzymatic reactions, the authors have developed a unique chemoenzymatic synthesis of triquinane sesquiterpenes. The enzymatic reactions would be difficult to replicate with synthetic methods, particularly the enantioselective Riley oxidation catalyzed by p450BM3 and the undirected methylene C-H hydroxylation catalyzed by PtlH. Thus, the use of enzymatic reactions in the chemoenzymatic synthesis is justifiable. Moreover, this is the first chemoenzymatic synthesis of this class of natural products, so the retrosynthetic strategy is a novel aspect of this work.
Despite being able to achieve enantioselective allylic C-H hydroxylation, the application to the synthesis of pentalenene is indirect. The hydroxyl group installed by enzymatic hydroxylation is removed by elimination to form the enone which renders the optimized dr of the hydroxylation inconsequential as the axial alcohol could also eliminate through an E2 reaction. Essentially, the primary purpose of the initial enzymatic step is to achieve a desymmetrization. The authors also compare their p450 hydroxylation method to synthetic reactions and mention that theirs is the first "direct" method for enantioselective allylic oxidation. While this reviewer agrees that this method allows for the direct installation of alcohols (OH) as opposed to other methods that incorporate acetate (OAc) or benzoyl (OBz) group, in the context of the synthesis, the acetate or the benzoyl group could be preferrable given that they are better leaving groups as the OH is eliminated to form an alkene. In addition, one of the benefits of asymmetric catalysis is that the enantiomer can also be synthesized by using the enantiomer of the ligand or catalyst.
The chemical steps include an unselective reduction of the cyclopropane to the gem dimethyl group which also resulted in the undesired reduction of the ketone to an alcohol. A selective oxidation of that alcohol back to the ketone was developed using tritylium tetrafluoroborate.
The PtlH C-H hydroxylation is a known reaction in the biosynthesis of pentalenolactone (Ref 59). This should be mentioned explicitly in the text. The PntE and PtlE regiodivergent Baeyer-Villiger (BV) oxidation have also been previously reported (Ref 60). This should also be mentioned explicitly in the text rather than attributing the identification of these enzymes to screening libraries for BV monooxygenases.
Given the potential applications of combining enzymatic reactions with chemical synthesis, this work is a significant example of biocatalysis enabled natural product synthesis. Moreover, this work utilizes both engineered and wild type biosynthetic enzymes at both early and late-stages of the synthesis. This reviewer believes this work could merit publication in Nature Communications if the authors expand on the enzymatic Riley oxidation. This reviewer recommends the following major revisions.
1. Can the authors through directed evolution of p450 enzymes access the enantiomer of 2 by selective oxidation of Hb2? If so, then this reviewer would agree that this would be consider an advance to the field of enantioselective allylic oxidation. This example would broaden the scope of this work and potentially allow for a chemoenzymatic synthesis pentalenic acid.
2. Can the authors through directed evolution of p450 enzymes access the diastereomer of 2 by selective oxidation of Ha1? The WT enzyme has 1.6:1 dr, so it should be possible to evolve the enzyme to achieve selectivity for the axial hydrogen. This alcohol could be more susceptible to elimination through E2 mechanism.
Some minor corrections and suggestions:
3. The yield of the p450 Riley oxidation should be provided in the Figures and main text rather than just in the methods section.
4. The authors should show a figure of the active site of p450BM3 and where the mutations in AAO4 are located. Are the mutations close to the heme co-factor?
5. Compound 14 is not a xanthate. It is a O-thiocarbamate.
6. In the methods sections, lysaste should be "lysate".

Because our substrate possesses a bowl-shaped, rigid scaffold, we anticipated that an enlarged active-site pocket would be required for efficient catalysis. The bulky phenylalanine at position 87 in the wild-type enzyme likely imposes significant steric hindrance. ## Abstract

Riley oxidation is a powerful method for introducing oxygen functionality but typically relies on toxic reagents and generally lacks enantiocontrol. This limitation has historically restricted the utility of this transformation for the direct asymmetric construction of complex scaffolds. Here, we show that fusion library screening and directed evolution enable the highly enantio- and diastereoselective Riley-type oxidation of a cis-diquinane substrate catalyzed by engineered P450 BM3. This enzymatic desymmetrization strategy provides streamlined access to key chiral cis-diquinane building block on a gram scale, facilitating rapid downstream diversification. Furthermore, by merging this enzymatic desymmetrization with chemical ring formation and late-stage biosynthetic oxidation, we achieve asymmetric total synthesis of pentalenolactone D and neo-pentalenolactone D. This work highlights the power of integrating protein engineering with synthetic chemistry to synthesis of complex natural products.

---

## Introduction

Natural products and drugs featuring a cis-diquinane scaffold typically possess architecturally complex frameworks and display notable biological activities1–5. Natural products containing the diquinane motif have long attracted the interest of synthetic chemists as targets for total synthesis6,7. However, efficient, and scalable preparation of chiral diquinane fragments remains a significant challenge. The C2-symmetric cis-diquinane core represents a meso framework that can, in principle, be efficiently accessed via desymmetrization strategies (Fig. 1A). Among previously reported strategies, desymmetrization by allylic oxidation has emerged as a powerful method for the synthesis of enantioenriched allylic alcohols (Fig. 1B)8–12. However, reported reactions of this type have thus far been limited to relatively simple substrates, and no examples of enantioselective Riley-type hydroxylation have been described to date13–21. Given the previous success of enzyme library screening and directed evolution strategies in synthetic applications22–34, we hypothesized that enzyme-catalyzed oxidation could offer a more effective solution for structurally complex substrates.

In this work, we develop a synthetic approach starting from an accessible, unsubstituted meso cis-diquinane, in which oxidative desymmetrization is employed to construct a chiral cis-diquinane core (Fig. 1C). This approach enables enantioselective Riley-type direct hydroxylation catalyzed by engineered P450 BM3. A readily accessible meso substrate bearing carbonyl and olefin functionalities serves as a versatile intermediate for downstream functionalization. Through subsequent side-chain installation, cyclization, and late-stage oxidation catalyzed by biosynthetic enzymes, this strategy provides access to the tricyclic skeleton and enables the asymmetric total synthesis of pentalenolactone D and neo-pentalenolactone D.

---

## Results

We selected the known compound 135 as a substrate to investigate the enzymatic desymmetrizing allylic oxidation (Fig. 2). By screening oxidative transformations using our oxidase libraries of P450 monooxygenases and α-ketoglutarate-dependent dioxygenases33, we identified that the wild-type P450 BM3 and its F87V mutant afforded the major hydroxylated product 2 with 73% e.e. and 1.6:1 d.r., 88% e.e. and 4.3: 1 d.r., respectively. Guided by the crystal structure of P450 BM3 (PDB: 1JPZ)36, we rationally selected and mutated several residues predicted to play critical roles in shaping the active-site pocket size and modulating substrate–residue interactions. Building upon the F87V mutant, we performed two rounds of saturation mutagenesis at residues 47 and 49. The resulting variant, AAO3, exhibited improved enantioselectivity and diastereoselectivity, affording compound 2 with 98% e.e. and 6.9:1 d.r. Mutations at positions 78 and 82 individually did not lead to further enhancement in selectivity. Inspired by Reetz’s strategy of combinatorial active-site mutagenesis37, we introduced a double mutation at these two positions. The resulting mutant, AAO4, significantly improved the diastereoselectivity (>20:1 d.r.) of the reaction while maintaining high enantioselectivity. We further achieved gram-scale synthesis of compound 2 with excellent diastereoselectivity and enantioselectivity. In addition, the absolute configuration of compound 2 was unambiguously confirmed by X-ray crystal structure of its derivative 4.

To showcase the applicability of the chiral cis-diquinane scaffold, we employed it in the total synthesis of pentalenolactone D and neo-pentalenolactone D3. Biological studies of the pentalenolactones have shown that they selectively inhibit glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate dehydrogenase, suggesting their potential as lead compounds for the development of novel antibiotic agents38–42. Accordingly, these pharmacologically important natural products have garnered significant attention from synthetic chemists43–60. Here, the retrosynthetic analysis of pentalenolactone D and neo-pentalenolactone D was undertaken (Fig. 3). Our retrosynthetic logic features a three-stage synthesis to access the target natural products. Initially, late-stage oxidation of biosynthetically recognizable 1-deoxypentalenic acid (7) enable the synthesis of pentalenolactones. In the next stage, 1-deoxypentalenic acid (7) can be obtained from pentalenene (8) via Riley oxidation. In addition, the skeleton of pentalenene (8) can be constructed by 9 through a sequence of Cu-catalyzed 1,4-addition and intramolecular alkylation. Compound 9 can be obtained from compound 2, generated via enzymatic desymmetrizing allylic oxidation, through an enantioretentive elimination. The key feature of this retrosynthetic analysis lies in the integration of engineered P450 BM3-catalyzed oxidation, chemical cyclization, and late-stage biosynthetic enzymatic oxidation.

Our synthetic route is depicted in Fig. 4, which commenced with commercially available compound 10. Although the synthesis of compound 1 had been previously reported via a three-step sequence35, we employed the method reported by H. Lebel and co-workers61 to access compound 1 directly from 10 in a single step, thereby improving step economy. With a substantial quantity of 1 in hand, compound 2 was prepared on a gram scale via our developed enzymatic desymmetrizing allylic oxidation, exhibiting high enantio- and diastereoselectivity. Simmons-Smith reaction of 2 afforded compound 11 which was subsequently subjected to hydrogenation to furnish the diol 12. Attempts to achieve selective oxidation of diol 12 to the compound 13 were undertaken. However, extensive screening of various oxidation conditions (DMP, PCC, SO3·Pyridine, etc.) lacked selectivity. Fortunately, treatment 12 with Ph3C+BF4- successfully afforded the desired compound 13 with excellent selectivity. The inability of the sterically congested carbocation to approach the hydroxyl group adjacent to the geminal dimethyl substituents may account for this observation. Then, we sought to dehydration of the C1-hydroxyl group of 13 to generate an alkene, followed by isomerization to afford enone 9. Presumably due to the presence of the geminal dimethyl group, dehydration reagents such as Burgess reagent and Martin sulfurane failed to yield the desired compound 9. Consequently, compound 13 was converted to the xanthate ester 14 and subsequent pyrolysis afforded 15. Notably, compound 15 underwent smoothly alkene isomerization under the condition to furnish enone 9. It is noteworthy that the elimination proceeded with retention of chirality. Conjugate addition to enone 9 proceeded smoothly, establishing the crucial quaternary carbon center. Subsequent desilylation afforded compound 16. Hydrogenation of 16 using Crabtree’s catalyst proceeded with moderate stereoselectivity, and the intermediate alcohol was tosylated to yield compound 17. Exposure of compound 17 under basic condition induced cyclization, affording the tricyclic product 18. Compound 18 was elaborated over two steps to furnish the natural product pentalenene (8). Pentalenene (8) was transformed to 1-deoxypentalenic acid (7) accessible to recognition by biosynthetic enzymes via allylic oxidation with SeO2, followed by Pinnick oxidation.

With 1-deoxypentalenic acid (7) in hand, we proceeded to investigate late-stage biosynthetic enzyme-catalyzed oxidation based on native enzymes originally reported by the group of D. E. Cane (Fig. 5)62,63. Among them, the α-ketoglutarate-dependent dioxygenase PtlH catalyzed hydroxylation at C11 of 1-deoxypentalenic acid (7), providing this transformation in high yield with exclusive regio- and stereoselectivity. Introduction the oxidation state is essential for achieving the total syntheses of pentalenolactone D (5) and neo-pentalenolactone D (6). Then, the resulting 19 was oxidized under Dess–Martin periodinane condition to provide ketone 20. Due to the observed instability of compound 20 on silica gel, it was carried forward without purification. Chemical Baeyer–Villiger oxidation conditions (m-CPBA, H2O2, etc.) proved unsatisfactory, which might be due to regioselectivity issues and incompatibility with the alkene moiety. Consequently, enzymatic Baeyer–Villiger oxidation was pursued. Screening of our Baeyer–Villiger monooxygenases library confirmed that the coexpression of PntE or PtlE, and the phosphite dehydrogenase Opt13 for NADPH (reduced form of nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide phosphate) regeneration in a single E. coli BL21(DE3) strain allowed remarkable regioselectivity to afford pentalenolactone D (5) and neo-pentalenolactone D (6), respectively. Other Baeyer–Villiger monooxygenases (AndJ, Rhodo, EthA, AusZ, etc), however, displayed no catalytic activity toward this substrate. Thus, through late-stage oxidation mediated by biosynthetic enzymes, we accomplished the asymmetric total syntheses of pentalenolactone D (5) and neo-pentalenolactone D (6).

## Methods

Generation of pET22b(+)-P450 BM3 and pRSF-Opt13 Co-expression Vector
The respective gene fragment of P450 BM3 was synthesized and assembled directly into pET22b(+) between NdeI and XhoI by Universe Gene Technology (Tianjin) Co. Ltd to yield vector pET22b(+)-P450 BM3. Opt-13 gene were inserted between NcoI and XhoI restriction sites of pRSF-1b to yield vector pRSF-Opt13. The resulting vectors pET22b(+)-P450 BM3 and pRSF-Opt13 were used to co-transform competent E. coli strain BL21(DE3).

Gram-Scale Synthesis of Compound 2
An overnight culture of E. coli BL21(DE3) cells harboring pET-22b(+)-based vector for expressing P450 BM3 (AAO4) and pRSF-Opt13 plasmid was used to inoculate 500 mL TB media (in 2L Erlenmeyer flask) containing 50 µg/mL kanamycin, 50 µg/mL ampicillin. The cultures were shaken at 250 rpm at 37 ˚C until an optical density of OD600=0.7–1.0 was reached. The cultures were cooled to 20°C (20 min) and then induced with 5-aminolevulinic, IPTG and FeSO4·7H2O to final concentrations of 1.0 mM, 0.5 mM and 0.05 mM, respectively. The cultures were shaken at 250 rpm at 20°C for a further 20 h. Cells were harvested by centrifugation (4°C, 15 min, 2100 × g), resuspended in 50 mM KPi (pH=8.00) to an OD600=10 into a 2L Erlenmeyer flask. Cells were disrupted by sonication (20 min, cycle= 1s on/2s off, 50% amplitude) and pelleted by centrifugation (4°C, 15 min, 2100 × g). The supernatant was used directly for subsequent reactions. Reactions were carried out in parallel across twelve 2L Erlenmeyer flasks, each charged with the following amounts of substrate and reagents. A pre-dissolved solution of 1 (300 mg, 2.0 mmol, 4.0 mM final concentration) in 25 mL DMSO was added to the lysate, followed by Na2NADP (250 mg, 0.32 mmol, 0.16 equiv.) and Na2HPO4∙5H2O (6.25 g, 28.9 mmol, 14.5 equiv.). The flask was shaken at 150 rpm at 23°C under air for 20 h. Then, 25 g NaCl was added to flask and the mixture was extracted with EtOAc (400 mL × 3). The combined organic extracts of twelve 2L Erlenmeyer flasks from the twelve parallel reactions were washed with sat. aq. NaHCO3 (400 mL), dried over anhydrous Na2SO4, and concentrated in vacuo. The crude material was purified by flash column chromatography to yield compound 2 of 1.60 g (44%) as yellow oil.

Furthermore, by merging this enzymatic desymmetrization with chemical ring formation and late-stage biosynthetic oxidation, we achieve asymmetric total synthesis of pentalenolactone D and neo-pentalenolactone D. This work highlights the power of integrating protein engineering with synthetic chemistry to synthesis of complex natural products.

## Introduction

Natural products and drugs featuring a cis-diquinane scaffold typically possess architecturally complex frameworks and display notable biological activities1–5. Natural products containing the diquinane motif have long attracted the interest of synthetic chemists as targets for total synthesis6,7. However, efficient, and scalable preparation of chiral diquinane fragments remains a significant challenge. The C2-symmetric cis-diquinane core represents a meso framework that can, in principle, be efficiently accessed via desymmetrization strategies (Fig. 1A). Among previously reported strategies, desymmetrization by allylic oxidation has emerged as a powerful method for the synthesis of enantioenriched allylic alcohols (Fig. 1B)8–12. However, reported reactions of this type have thus far been limited to relatively simple substrates, and no examples of enantioselective Riley-type hydroxylation have been described to date13–21. Given the previous success of enzyme library screening and directed evolution strategies in synthetic applications22–34, we hypothesized that enzyme-catalyzed oxidation could offer a more effective solution for structurally complex substrates.

In this work, we develop a synthetic approach starting from an accessible, unsubstituted meso cis-diquinane, in which oxidative desymmetrization is employed to construct a chiral cis-diquinane core (Fig. 1C). This approach enables enantioselective Riley-type direct hydroxylation catalyzed by engineered P450 BM3. A readily accessible meso substrate bearing carbonyl and olefin functionalities serves as a versatile intermediate for downstream functionalization. Through subsequent side-chain installation, cyclization, and late-stage oxidation catalyzed by biosynthetic enzymes, this strategy provides access to the tricyclic skeleton and enables the asymmetric total synthesis of pentalenolactone D and neo-pentalenolactone D.

## Results

We selected the known compound 135 as a substrate to investigate the enzymatic desymmetrizing allylic oxidation (Fig. 2). By screening oxidative transformations using our oxidase libraries of P450 monooxygenases and α-ketoglutarate-dependent dioxygenases33, we identified that the wild-type P450 BM3 and its F87V mutant afforded the major hydroxylated product 2 with 73% e.e. and 1.6:1 d.r., 88% e.e. and 4.3: 1 d.r., respectively. Guided by the crystal structure of P450 BM3 (PDB: 1JPZ)36, we rationally selected and mutated several residues predicted to play critical roles in shaping the active-site pocket size and modulating substrate–residue interactions. Building upon the F87V mutant, we performed two rounds of saturation mutagenesis at residues 47 and 49. The resulting variant, AAO3, exhibited improved enantioselectivity and diastereoselectivity, affording compound 2 with 98% e.e. and 6.9:1 d.r. Mutations at positions 78 and 82 individually did not lead to further enhancement in selectivity. Inspired by Reetz’s strategy of combinatorial active-site mutagenesis37, we introduced a double mutation at these two positions. The resulting mutant, AAO4, significantly improved the diastereoselectivity (>20:1 d.r.) of the reaction while maintaining high enantioselectivity. We further achieved gram-scale synthesis of compound 2 with excellent diastereoselectivity and enantioselectivity. In addition, the absolute configuration of compound 2 was unambiguously confirmed by X-ray crystal structure of its derivative 4.

To showcase the applicability of the chiral cis-diquinane scaffold, we employed it in the total synthesis of pentalenolactone D and neo-pentalenolactone D3. Biological studies of the pentalenolactones have shown that they selectively inhibit glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate dehydrogenase, suggesting their potential as lead compounds for the development of novel antibiotic agents38–42. Accordingly, these pharmacologically important natural products have garnered significant attention from synthetic chemists43–60. Here, the retrosynthetic analysis of pentalenolactone D and neo-pentalenolactone D was undertaken (Fig. 3). Our retrosynthetic logic features a three-stage synthesis to access the target natural products. Initially, late-stage oxidation of biosynthetically recognizable 1-deoxypentalenic acid (7) enable the synthesis of pentalenolactones. In the next stage, 1-deoxypentalenic acid (7) can be obtained from pentalenene (8) via Riley oxidation. In addition, the skeleton of pentalenene (8) can be constructed by 9 through a sequence of Cu-catalyzed 1,4-addition and intramolecular alkylation. Compound 9 can be obtained from compound 2, generated via enzymatic desymmetrizing allylic oxidation, through an enantioretentive elimination. The key feature of this retrosynthetic analysis lies in the integration of engineered P450 BM3-catalyzed oxidation, chemical cyclization, and late-stage biosynthetic enzymatic oxidation.

Our synthetic route is depicted in Fig. 4, which commenced with commercially available compound 10. Although the synthesis of compound 1 had been previously reported via a three-step sequence35, we employed the method reported by H. Lebel and co-workers61 to access compound 1 directly from 10 in a single step, thereby improving step economy. With a substantial quantity of 1 in hand, compound 2 was prepared on a gram scale via our developed enzymatic desymmetrizing allylic oxidation, exhibiting high enantio- and diastereoselectivity. Simmons-Smith reaction of 2 afforded compound 11 which was subsequently subjected to hydrogenation to furnish the diol 12. Attempts to achieve selective oxidation of diol 12 to the compound 13 were undertaken. However, extensive screening of various oxidation conditions (DMP, PCC, SO3·Pyridine, etc.) lacked selectivity. Fortunately, treatment 12 with Ph3C+BF4- successfully afforded the desired compound 13 with excellent selectivity. The inability of the sterically congested carbocation to approach the hydroxyl group adjacent to the geminal dimethyl substituents may account for this observation. Then, we sought to dehydration of the C1-hydroxyl group of 13 to generate an alkene, followed by isomerization to afford enone 9. Presumably due to the presence of the geminal dimethyl group, dehydration reagents such as Burgess reagent and Martin sulfurane failed to yield the desired compound 9. Consequently, compound 13 was converted to the xanthate ester 14 and subsequent pyrolysis afforded 15. Notably, compound 15 underwent smoothly alkene isomerization under the condition to furnish enone 9. It is noteworthy that the elimination proceeded with retention of chirality. Conjugate addition to enone 9 proceeded smoothly, establishing the crucial quaternary carbon center. Subsequent desilylation afforded compound 16. Hydrogenation of 16 using Crabtree’s catalyst proceeded with moderate stereoselectivity, and the intermediate alcohol was tosylated to yield compound 17. Exposure of compound 17 under basic condition induced cyclization, affording the tricyclic product 18. Compound 18 was elaborated over two steps to furnish the natural product pentalenene (8). Pentalenene (8) was transformed to 1-deoxypentalenic acid (7) accessible to recognition by biosynthetic enzymes via allylic oxidation with SeO2, followed by Pinnick oxidation.

With 1-deoxypentalenic acid (7) in hand, we proceeded to investigate late-stage biosynthetic enzyme-catalyzed oxidation based on native enzymes originally reported by the group of D. E. Cane (Fig. 5)62,63. Among them, the α-ketoglutarate-dependent dioxygenase PtlH catalyzed hydroxylation at C11 of 1-deoxypentalenic acid (7), providing this transformation in high yield with exclusive regio- and stereoselectivity. Introduction the oxidation state is essential for achieving the total syntheses of pentalenolactone D (5) and neo-pentalenolactone D (6). Then, the resulting 19 was oxidized under Dess–Martin periodinane condition to provide ketone 20. Due to the observed instability of compound 20 on silica gel, it was carried forward without purification. Chemical Baeyer–Villiger oxidation conditions (m-CPBA, H2O2, etc.) proved unsatisfactory, which might be due to regioselectivity issues and incompatibility with the alkene moiety. Consequently, enzymatic Baeyer–Villiger oxidation was pursued. Screening of our Baeyer–Villiger monooxygenases library confirmed that the coexpression of PntE or PtlE, and the phosphite dehydrogenase Opt13 for NADPH (reduced form of nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide phosphate) regeneration in a single E. coli BL21(DE3) strain allowed remarkable regioselectivity to afford pentalenolactone D (5) and neo-pentalenolactone D (6), respectively. Other Baeyer–Villiger monooxygenases (AndJ, Rhodo, EthA, AusZ, etc), however, displayed no catalytic activity toward this substrate. Thus, through late-stage oxidation mediated by biosynthetic enzymes, we accomplished the asymmetric total syntheses of pentalenolactone D (5) and neo-pentalenolactone D (6).

## Methods

Generation of pET22b(+)-P450 BM3 and pRSF-Opt13 Co-expression Vector
The respective gene fragment of P450 BM3 was synthesized and assembled directly into pET22b(+) between NdeI and XhoI by Universe Gene Technology (Tianjin) Co. Ltd to yield vector pET22b(+)-P450 BM3. Opt-13 gene were inserted between NcoI and XhoI restriction sites of pRSF-1b to yield vector pRSF-Opt13. The resulting vectors pET22b(+)-P450 BM3 and pRSF-Opt13 were used to co-transform competent E. coli strain BL21(DE3).

Gram-Scale Synthesis of Compound 2
An overnight culture of E. coli BL21(DE3) cells harboring pET-22b(+)-based vector for expressing P450 BM3 (AAO4) and pRSF-Opt13 plasmid was used to inoculate 500 mL TB media (in 2L Erlenmeyer flask) containing 50 µg/mL kanamycin, 50 µg/mL ampicillin. The cultures were shaken at 250 rpm at 37 ˚C until an optical density of OD600=0.7–1.0 was reached. The cultures were cooled to 20°C (20 min) and then induced with 5-aminolevulinic, IPTG and FeSO4·7H2O to final concentrations of 1.0 mM, 0.5 mM and 0.05 mM, respectively. The cultures were shaken at 250 rpm at 20°C for a further 20 h. Cells were harvested by centrifugation (4°C, 15 min, 2100 × g), resuspended in 50 mM KPi (pH=8.00) to an OD600=10 into a 2L Erlenmeyer flask. Cells were disrupted by sonication (20 min, cycle= 1s on/2s off, 50% amplitude) and pelleted by centrifugation (4°C, 15 min, 2100 × g). The supernatant was used directly for subsequent reactions. Reactions were carried out in parallel across twelve 2L Erlenmeyer flasks, each charged with the following amounts of substrate and reagents. A pre-dissolved solution of 1 (300 mg, 2.0 mmol, 4.0 mM final concentration) in 25 mL DMSO was added to the lysate, followed by Na2NADP (250 mg, 0.32 mmol, 0.16 equiv.) and Na2HPO4∙5H2O (6.25 g, 28.9 mmol, 14.5 equiv.). The flask was shaken at 150 rpm at 23°C under air for 20 h. Then, 25 g NaCl was added to flask and the mixture was extracted with EtOAc (400 mL × 3). The combined organic extracts of twelve 2L Erlenmeyer flasks from the twelve parallel reactions were washed with sat. aq. NaHCO3 (400 mL), dried over anhydrous Na2SO4, and concentrated in vacuo. The crude material was purified by flash column chromatography to yield compound 2 of 1.60 g (44%) as yellow oil.

## Paper

## Abstract

Riley oxidation is a powerful method for introducing oxygen functionality but typically relies on toxic reagents and generally lacks enantiocontrol. This limitation has historically restricted the utility of this transformation for the direct asymmetric construction of complex scaffolds. Here, we show that fusion library screening and directed evolution enable the highly enantio- and diastereoselective Riley-type oxidation of a cis-diquinane substrate catalyzed by engineered P450 BM3. This enzymatic desymmetrization strategy provides streamlined access to key chiral cis-diquinane building block on a gram scale, facilitating rapid downstream diversification. Furthermore, by merging this enzymatic desymmetrization with chemical ring formation and late-stage biosynthetic oxidation, we achieve asymmetric total synthesis of pentalenolactone D and neo-pentalenolactone D. This work highlights the power of integrating protein engineering with synthetic chemistry to synthesis of complex natural products.

---

## Introduction

Natural products and drugs featuring a cis-diquinane scaffold typically possess architecturally complex frameworks and display notable biological activities1–5. Natural products containing the diquinane motif have long attracted the interest of synthetic chemists as targets for total synthesis6,7. However, efficient, and scalable preparation of chiral diquinane fragments remains a significant challenge. The C2-symmetric cis-diquinane core represents a meso framework that can, in principle, be efficiently accessed via desymmetrization strategies (Fig. 1A). Among previously reported strategies, desymmetrization by allylic oxidation has emerged as a powerful method for the synthesis of enantioenriched allylic alcohols (Fig. 1B)8–12. However, reported reactions of this type have thus far been limited to relatively simple substrates, and no examples of enantioselective Riley-type hydroxylation have been described to date13–21. Given the previous success of enzyme library screening and directed evolution strategies in synthetic applications22–34, we hypothesized that enzyme-catalyzed oxidation could offer a more effective solution for structurally complex substrates.

In this work, we develop a synthetic approach starting from an accessible, unsubstituted meso cis-diquinane, in which oxidative desymmetrization is employed to construct a chiral cis-diquinane core (Fig. 1C). This approach enables enantioselective Riley-type direct hydroxylation catalyzed by engineered P450 BM3. A readily accessible meso substrate bearing carbonyl and olefin functionalities serves as a versatile intermediate for downstream functionalization. Through subsequent side-chain installation, cyclization, and late-stage oxidation catalyzed by biosynthetic enzymes, this strategy provides access to the tricyclic skeleton and enables the asymmetric total synthesis of pentalenolactone D and neo-pentalenolactone D.

---

We selected the known compound 135 as a substrate to investigate the enzymatic desymmetrizing allylic oxidation (Fig. 2). By screening oxidative transformations using our oxidase libraries of P450 monooxygenases and α-ketoglutarate-dependent dioxygenases33, we identified that the wild-type P450 BM3 and its F87V mutant afforded the major hydroxylated product 2 with 73% e.e. and 1.6:1 d.r., 88% e.e. and 4.3: 1 d.r., respectively. Guided by the crystal structure of P450 BM3 (PDB: 1JPZ)36, we rationally selected and mutated several residues predicted to play critical roles in shaping the active-site pocket size and modulating substrate–residue interactions. Building upon the F87V mutant, we performed two rounds of saturation mutagenesis at residues 47 and 49. The resulting variant, AAO3, exhibited improved enantioselectivity and diastereoselectivity, affording compound 2 with 98% e.e. and 6.9:1 d.r. Mutations at positions 78 and 82 individually did not lead to further enhancement in selectivity. Inspired by Reetz’s strategy of combinatorial active-site mutagenesis37, we introduced a double mutation at these two positions. The resulting mutant, AAO4, significantly improved the diastereoselectivity (>20:1 d.r.) of the reaction while maintaining high enantioselectivity. We further achieved gram-scale synthesis of compound 2 with excellent diastereoselectivity and enantioselectivity. In addition, the absolute configuration of compound 2 was unambiguously confirmed by X-ray crystal structure of its derivative 4.

To showcase the applicability of the chiral cis-diquinane scaffold, we employed it in the total synthesis of pentalenolactone D and neo-pentalenolactone D3. Biological studies of the pentalenolactones have shown that they selectively inhibit glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate dehydrogenase, suggesting their potential as lead compounds for the development of novel antibiotic agents38–42. Our retrosynthetic logic features a three-stage synthesis to access the target natural products. Initially, late-stage oxidation of biosynthetically recognizable 1-deoxypentalenic acid (7) enable the synthesis of pentalenolactones. In the next stage, 1-deoxypentalenic acid (7) can be obtained from pentalenene (8) via Riley oxidation. Generation of pET22b(+)-P450 BM3 and pRSF-Opt13 Co-expression Vector
The respective gene fragment of P450 BM3 was synthesized and assembled directly into pET22b(+) between NdeI and XhoI by Universe Gene Technology (Tianjin) Co. Ltd to yield vector pET22b(+)-P450 BM3. Comments:
The authors report a chemoenzymatic synthesis of pentalenolactone D and its regioisomer neo-pentalenolactone D. First, the authors utilize a p450BM3 enzyme and through directed evolution achieve highly selective desymmetrization of diquinanes by enzymatic Riley oxidation. Second, chemical synthesis is used for a concise synthesis of triquinanes pentalenene and 1-deoxypentalenic acid. Finally, using known biosynthetic enzymes in the biosynthesis of pentalenolactone, the chemoenzymatic synthesis was achieved. These enzymes include an alpha-KG dependent hydroxylase, PtlH, and the regiodivergent Baeyer-Villiger monooxygenases (PntE and PtlE).
By combining synthetic chemistry with enzymatic reactions, the authors have developed a unique chemoenzymatic synthesis of triquinane sesquiterpenes. The enzymatic reactions would be difficult to replicate with synthetic methods, particularly the enantioselective Riley oxidation catalyzed by p450BM3 and the undirected methylene C-H hydroxylation catalyzed by PtlH. Thus, the use of enzymatic reactions in the chemoenzymatic synthesis is justifiable. Moreover, this is the first chemoenzymatic synthesis of this class of natural products, so the retrosynthetic strategy is a novel aspect of this work.
Despite being able to achieve enantioselective allylic C-H hydroxylation, the application to the synthesis of pentalenene is indirect. The hydroxyl group installed by enzymatic hydroxylation is removed by elimination to form the enone which renders the optimized dr of the hydroxylation inconsequential as the axial alcohol could also eliminate through an E2 reaction. Essentially, the primary purpose of the initial enzymatic step is to achieve a desymmetrization. The authors also compare their p450 hydroxylation method to synthetic reactions and mention that theirs is the first "direct" method for enantioselective allylic oxidation. While this reviewer agrees that this method allows for the direct installation of alcohols (OH) as opposed to other methods that incorporate acetate (OAc) or benzoyl (OBz) group, in the context of the synthesis, the acetate or the benzoyl group could be preferrable given that they are better leaving groups as the OH is eliminated to form an alkene. In addition, one of the benefits of asymmetric catalysis is that the enantiomer can also be synthesized by using the enantiomer of the ligand or catalyst.
The chemical steps include an unselective reduction of the cyclopropane to the gem dimethyl group which also resulted in the undesired reduction of the ketone to an alcohol. A selective oxidation of that alcohol back to the ketone was developed using tritylium tetrafluoroborate.
The PtlH C-H hydroxylation is a known reaction in the biosynthesis of pentalenolactone (Ref 59). This should be mentioned explicitly in the text. The PntE and PtlE regiodivergent Baeyer-Villiger (BV) oxidation have also been previously reported (Ref 60). This should also be mentioned explicitly in the text rather than attributing the identification of these enzymes to screening libraries for BV monooxygenases.
Given the potential applications of combining enzymatic reactions with chemical synthesis, this work is a significant example of biocatalysis enabled natural product synthesis. Moreover, this work utilizes both engineered and wild type biosynthetic enzymes at both early and late-stages of the synthesis. This reviewer believes this work could merit publication in Nature Communications if the authors expand on the enzymatic Riley oxidation. This reviewer recommends the following major revisions.
